title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
claim: A learned parent feature decomposes into finer child features, showing the model recovers an interpretable semantic hierarchy.
layout: 4 boxes: one wide parent on top, three child boxes below; color-coded borders
description: The figure shows four rounded boxes with gray title bars. A wide box at the top, with a bright blue border, is titled 'Expert #858'. It lists five text snippets from a corpus. Wedding-related tokens in them are underlined and bolded, for example 'nuptials', 'betrothed' and 'Shaadi'. Below it sit three smaller boxes in a row: 'Sublatent 2' with a navy border, 'Sublatent 4' with a teal border, and 'Sublatent 11' with a periwinkle border. Each lists five snippets in smaller monospace type. Sublatent 2 covers divorce, Sublatent 4 covers engagement and honeymoon, and Sublatent 11 covers marriage and bridal. Underline colors match the box borders. Bold text marks stronger activation. No arrows are drawn, but the layout implies a parent-to-children hierarchy. The eye goes first to the large top box.
caption: A Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder architecture learns human interpretable hierarchy. Each box shows 5 of the strongest activating contexts for the feature, all tokens underlined activate the feature while the bold/text weight shows the relative strength of activation. For example, a "marriage" high-level feature and "divorce", "engagement", and "marriage" sublatents. Note that "48 sati svadba" is a Serbian wedding reality TV show and "Shaadi" is the Hindi word for marriage.
abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.
